questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what a grant of land did and did not transfer
questions.stem: A lord grants a holding in land to a knight for his lifetime, with service owed. What did the grant actually convey?

options.text: Possession on condition of service, with the grant lapsing if the terms were broken
Permanent and unconditional ownership that no later service could take back
options.misconception: believes a fief made the grantee absolute owner in perpetuity

options.text: A salary paid in cash out of the lord's household accounts every year
options.misconception: confuses a land-based grant with a money wage

options.text: A share of the lord's power to judge everyone inside the parish boundary
options.misconception: confuses land tenure with delegated jurisdiction

questions.explanation: A fief conveyed possession on terms: the holder owed service and the holding returned to the lord if the heirs failed or the service went unpaid, so a right of reversion survived every transfer. Ownership in perpetuity denies the condition, a cash salary denies the land, and judicial authority was granted separately and often withheld.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the holding when the service stopped.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: describe the reciprocal duties sealed by homage
questions.stem: A vassal kneels, lays his joined hands in his lord's hands, and swears faith. Which exchange does the rite of homage actually record?

options.text: The vassal's oath of service in return for the lord's gift and undertaking of protection
The vassal's absolute surrender of every other duty he owed anyone else
options.misconception: believes homage wiped out obligations owed outside the tie

options.text: The lord's promise to pay the vassal a fixed yearly sum in coined silver
options.misconception: confuses homage with a money pension

options.text: The surrender of the vassal's land into the lord's own demesne for safekeeping
options.misconception: confuses the oath ceremony with a confiscation of property

questions.explanation: Homage was bilateral: the vassal swore service and the lord undertook to protect the vassal's person and lands, so the tie bound both sides. An absolute surrender, a cash annuity, and a deposit of land each break that pair, keeping one half and dropping the other.
questions.hint: One side promises service; what does the other side promise?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the feudal bond had teeth
questions.learningObjective: explain why conditional landholding produced reliable service
questions.stem: A ruler fields an army by granting land for service instead of paying soldiers a wage. Why is this arrangement a reliable way to raise troops?

options.text: The grant ends with the service, so a defaulter risks at once the estate his standing rests on
Landholders need no drill, because farming has already taught every one of them to fight
options.misconception: assumes a martial skill that holding land did not create

options.text: A royal payroll costs less than feeding any army once it is in the field
options.misconception: compares two costs while ignoring the forfeiture

options.text: Service was paid in land because soldiers had no property of their own to lose
options.misconception: reverses cause and effect between service and tenure

questions.explanation: Tenure made service self-enforcing: the moment a holder stopped serving he risked the estate his status rested on, so obedience and self-interest pointed the same way. Farming teaches nobody to fight, a payroll comparison sets aside the forfeiture, and the third choice has the cause and effect the wrong way round.
questions.hint: What does a rebel lose that a hired soldier could keep?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a charter of homage records
questions.learningObjective: read a charter summary for the clause that carries the obligation
questions.stem: A summary of a twelfth-century charter records that the grantee gave his oath of faith to the lord, promised service in his own person, and accepted that the holding reverts if he dies without a legitimate heir.

options.text: The binding element is the condition, since the grant stands only while oath and heir rule hold
The binding element is the homage alone, which by itself fixed the whole term
options.misconception: reads a single formula as if it settled everything

options.text: The binding element is the personal service, which had to be repeated in writing each year
options.misconception: thinks a life tenure needed a written renewal annually

options.text: The binding element is the heir rule, which overrode the lord's own right to decide
options.misconception: reverses who held the right of reversion

questions.explanation: The charter is a conditional grant: faith, personal service, and the heir rule together make the holding lapse, so the condition is the binding element. Homage alone leaves the service clause unexplained, an annual written renewal contradicts a term ending in death, and the reversion belonged to the lord rather than to the heir rule.
questions.hint: Which clause in the summary would a lawyer call the condition?

questions.topic: Benefice and fief side by side
questions.learningObjective: contrast a clerical holding with a lay one
questions.stem: A bishop gives a priest a parcel of land to live on while he serves the parish. Which feature most sharply separates this grant from a lay fief?

options.text: The holding passes to the next appointee rather than to the priest's own heirs
The holder is chosen by the parish congregation instead of by any superior
options.misconception: believes parish election founded the benefice system

options.text: The land is worked by hired hands, so the priest draws no income from it at all
options.misconception: confuses a benefice with the lord's demesne

options.text: The grant runs for one year and is renewed whenever the priest requests it
options.misconception: confuses a benefice with a short lease

questions.explanation: A benefice supported a cleric in his office: the income attached to the office rather than to the man, so it could not be inherited or given away. Election by the congregation, hired farming with no income, and a single-year term each describe arrangements the benefice did not use.
questions.hint: Ask whether the priest's sons could have kept the land.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how subdividing a fief shortened the ruler's direct authority
questions.stem: A great baron takes one vast fief and grants pieces of it to fifty lesser knights, each of whom swears to him. What follows for the crown?

options.text: The crown must now deal with fifty vassals whose first loyalty was pledged to the baron
The crown gains fifty more sworn supporters who are bound to it directly
options.misconception: counts the new knights as vassals of the crown

options.text: The baron's own land grows too scattered for him to defend or work alone
options.misconception: supposes subdivision weakens the baron rather than the crown

options.text: Every new knight owes the crown service, because land is held from the king by nature
options.misconception: mistakes a private grant for a grant from the crown

questions.explanation: Subinfeudation inserted a rank between the crown and the field: the lesser knight's oath bound him to the baron, so the distance between king and soldier grew. Counting the new knights as royal vassals, supposing subdivision punished the baron, and treating all land as royal in origin each mistake a private regrant for a royal one.
questions.hint: Ask who received the first oath of service.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the demesne mattered to a lord
questions.learningObjective: explain the lord's own farming as the base of seigneurial wealth
questions.stem: A lord keeps a large block of land under his own control and worked by his own servants. Why was that arrangement central to his wealth?

options.text: Because its surplus paid retainers, clerks, and the displays that advertised a lord's rank
Because it let the lord keep every acre off the rolls and so escape taxation
options.misconception: believes the demesne existed chiefly to dodge dues

options.text: Because the peasants' strips were worked harder than the lord's own ploughland
options.misconception: assumes peasant strips outperformed the demesne

options.text: Because demesne land stood outside the court that heard disputes on the manor
options.misconception: invents a court exemption the manor never had

questions.explanation: The demesne was the lord's own farm, and the surplus it produced was spent on followers, priests, and status, which is the wealth that made lordship worth defending at all. Tax avoidance, better peasant strips, and a court exemption each detach the arrangement from the income it generated.
questions.hint: Ask who received the first slice of the demesne harvest.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Was feudalism a contract or a hierarchy
questions.learningObjective: weigh a contractual reading of vassalage against a social one
questions.stem: One reading treats medieval vassalage as a bargain in which both sides gained protection and land; another treats it as a society of subordination in which one side gave everything. Which best fits the evidence?

options.text: A bargain in form whose substance was one-sided, since the lord set the terms and could withdraw the grant
A pure contract, because mutual promises bound the lord exactly as they bound the vassal
options.misconception: takes the form of consent for equality of power

options.text: Pure subordination, because no medieval person thought of the tie as an agreement at all
options.misconception: erases the oath that the ceremony actually performed

options.text: Neither, because the vocabulary of service in the Middle Ages had no legal effect whatever
options.misconception: treats feudal law as empty rhetoric

questions.explanation: The rite really was an agreement and the land really was held on terms, so the contractual reading gets the form right; but the lord chose the terms, withheld confirmation, and recovered the holding on failure, so the substance was one-sided. Taking the form at face value, denying that anyone made an oath, and emptying the language of law each discard evidence that is actually there.
questions.hint: Ask who drafted the terms and who could withdraw them.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Labour services counted on a manor
questions.learningObjective: compute the total days of service a set of holdings required
questions.stem: A manor roll records that each of twenty holdings owes three days of ploughing at Michaelmas. How many days of service does the village owe altogether?

options.text: 60 days, since twenty holdings at three days each give twenty times three
23 days, since three days across twenty holdings averages under two days apiece
options.misconception: averages instead of multiplying a stated obligation

options.text: 200 days, since the roll's twenty entries each carry ten days of ploughing
options.misconception: reads the count of holdings as a different days figure

options.text: 9 days, since only three of the twenty holdings appear in this roll entry
options.misconception: counts the number three as if it were a count of holdings

questions.explanation: The roll states three days per holding for twenty holdings, so the total is a multiplication: 20 x 3 = 60. Averaging a per-holding term treats it as a per-village one, the 200 result invents a ten-day figure, and 9 mistakes the term three for a count of holdings.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of holdings by the days owed on each.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: recall the chief function of the lord's own court
questions.stem: Disputes over a strip of ploughland, a boundary, and a tenant's rent are brought before a court held on the manor. What is that court chiefly for?

options.text: Settling local disputes and enforcing the lord's own customary law upon his tenants
Hearing appeals from the king's central courts in the county town
options.misconception: believes the manorial court sat above the royal courts

options.text: Choosing the priest, the reeve, and the parish constable once each year
options.misconception: confuses church appointment with manorial jurisdiction

options.text: Registering every birth, marriage, and death in the parish for the year
options.misconception: confuses parish registers with manorial business

questions.explanation: The manorial court was the lord's own local jurisdiction over the people who lived on his land, applying the customs the community had always used, which is why a rent dispute could end there. It sat below the royal courts, it did not appoint the priest, and parish registers were a separate record.
questions.hint: Ask whose law the court applied and over whom.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The three courses of a village field
questions.learningObjective: recall what the open-field rotation accomplished
questions.stem: A village's ploughland is divided into long strips and the whole field is ploughed in three turns: one autumn sowing, one spring sowing, one fallow. What does that rotation accomplish?

options.text: It spreads the work and the feeding of both ploughland and herds across the whole village
It leaves each household with one undivided strip that nobody else can plough
options.misconception: confuses open strips with consolidated holdings

options.text: It sets aside the best ground for permanent cultivation by the lord alone
options.misconception: turns an open system into a demesne monopoly

options.text: It frees the village from any need to keep livestock on the ploughland at all
options.misconception: drops the fallow that fed the animals

questions.explanation: The three-course system divided the ploughland so that part was sown, part rested, and part carried the animals, which is what made both grain and herds possible with scarce labour. Consolidated private strips, a lord's permanent monopoly, and a fallow removed each undo the arrangement the rotation exists to manage.
questions.hint: Ask what the fallow turn was doing in the field.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why services were commuted into cash rents
questions.stem: Across two centuries more peasants pay a fixed cash rent where their forefathers worked the lord's fields. What change in the countryside made that substitution possible?

options.text: Growing markets made labour scarce, so a lord could buy the work instead of compelling it
A shrinking money supply forced payment in whatever the manor had to spare
options.misconception: explains cash rents by an absence of coin

options.text: A legal decree forbade working the lord's land and demanded rent instead
options.misconception: invents a statute that abolished the old service outright

options.text: Serfdom arriving from the east required wages to replace labour services
options.misconception: reverses the direction in which labour control moved

questions.explanation: Cash rent took over where labour had grown expensive and unreliable as population and markets grew, so a lord could buy the work rather than compel it. A vanishing money supply would push towards payment in kind, no decree abolished the old service, and eastern serfdom tightened labour control rather than relaxing it.
questions.hint: Ask what a lord does when hands are scarce and wages are cheap.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Population growth and the terms of tenure
questions.learningObjective: reason from demographic growth to pressure on customary tenure
questions.stem: After a long run of good harvests, village wages rise and land values climb. Why does that combination hurt the lord in particular?

options.text: Custom pinned peasants to old terms just as their own bargaining power finally improved
A richer village is taxed twice, once by the lord and once by the king
options.misconception: invents a double tax that demographic growth did not create

options.text: Rising wages raise the lord's own food bill, which he pays to the same men
options.misconception: sees a cost effect and misses the tenure effect

options.text: Population growth lets the king out-collect the lord from a land tax
options.misconception: moves the argument to royal revenue instead of lordly income

questions.explanation: Customary tenure held the peasant to old terms precisely when his position improved, and wages and land values rising together were that improvement made visible, so the lord's income lagged while the household's rose. A double tax, a cost effect on the lord's own purchases, and a shift to royal revenue all miss that the price of the holding had been fixed by custom.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the bargain custom kept unchanged.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a manorial court roll shows
questions.learningObjective: infer the machinery behind an entry in a court roll
questions.stem: A roll summary records that the reeve presented twelve defaulting tenants, that sworn neighbours vetted two men as good and lawful, and that a strip boundary was marked with a stone and entered in the court.

options.text: The court ran through presentment and recorded findings, which is how custom became enforceable
The court sat as a full parliament with elected representatives of the county
options.misconception: reads a jury presentment as parliamentary representation

options.text: The court functioned as a royal court giving authority to the king's own judges
options.misconception: reverses which of the two courts outranked the other

options.text: The roll was a survey of the fields made during the lord's own inspection
options.misconception: reads a record of hearings as a tour of the estate

questions.explanation: An entry like this shows a working local court: a reeve presenting cases, neighbours vetting suitors, and a decision entered so that it could not be reopened, which is how an unwritten custom became an enforceable rule. It was not a parliament, it did not outrank the crown's courts, and it is not an inspection of the fields.
questions.hint: Ask what the sworn neighbours did with the names they presented.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: describe how a manor jury identified culprits
questions.stem: A manor is asking neighbours to name who cut hedges, drove cattle off common pasture, or broke a rule of the wood. What is this collective accusation called?

options.text: The vill's presentment, in which sworn neighbours name suspects before the court
The lord's homage, in which tenants pledge service in return for protection
options.misconception: confuses a presentment with the vassal's oath

options.text: The king's eyre, in which royal justices tour the county holding pleas
options.misconception: confuses a local jury with a royal circuit

options.text: The commenda, in which partners share the risk and the profit of a voyage
options.misconception: confuses court business with a trading contract

questions.explanation: The vill's presentment was the sworn neighbours' charge: they named those they had seen break the rules and the court then judged, so the guilt was established by the community before the lord heard it. It is not the vassal's oath, not a circuit of royal justices, and not a form of trading agreement.
questions.hint: Ask who was doing the accusing, and in which room.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: compare the pace of unfree labour obligations across Europe
questions.stem: Peasant dues in the west had commuted to cash by about 1200, while in the east land was granted on terms binding whole villages to their lord. How should that difference be explained?

options.text: Denser settlement, scarcer labour, and stronger west European towns, which forced lords to pay for workers
Two different races of serf, one born to bondage and the other to liberty
options.misconception: falls back on inherited difference to explain an economic one

options.text: An eastern legal code that abolished the money rent the west had adopted
options.misconception: makes a statute do what population and wages did

options.text: A single western decree that ended villeinage across the whole kingdom
options.misconception: believes one decree ended western service

questions.explanation: Where labour was scarce and markets dense, lords had to attract and pay workers rather than compel them, and that is why western services commuted first while eastern lords could still bind a village. Distinct races, an eastern statute, and a single western decree each substitute one invented cause for the economic pressure the two regions actually met with different intensity.
questions.hint: Ask what a lord in a dense labour market had to do to get hands.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why an unwritten custom was still reliable law
questions.stem: A tenant disputes a rent and quotes what his neighbours have always paid, though no written deed for it exists. Why can the court still settle the dispute?

options.text: Because the custom was held in the memory of the whole community and enforced as a shared right
Because oral testimony always outweighs a written deed in a manor court
options.misconception: replaces a legal rule with a general rule about evidence

options.text: Because the lord's own memory fixed the rent and the court simply obeyed him
options.misconception: turns a community custom into the lord's private recollection

options.text: Because the church kept a written register of every rent owed in the village
options.misconception: invents a written parochial register of rents

questions.explanation: Unwritten custom worked because it was a standard the whole community remembered, so neighbours could testify to it and a court could apply it without a deed while the tenant could rely on it. Oral beats written only as a general rule of evidence, a lord's private memory is not a community custom, and no church register held manor rents.
questions.hint: Ask who else besides the tenant knew the rent.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The wages ordinance as a ceiling
questions.learningObjective: explain why a wage ceiling failed after a demographic catastrophe
questions.stem: After a plague has killed a third of the population, a government fixes the day's wage at the old rate and fines every employer who pays more. What happens, and why?

options.text: Wages stay high, because with a third of the workers gone the remaining hands set the price
Wages fall to the legal rate at once, since the threat of a fine forces instant obedience
options.misconception: assumes a penalty can conjure up labour the countryside has lost

options.text: Wages fall and output rises, since fewer workers must mean each one works harder
options.misconception: confuses a shortage of labour with a surplus of it

options.text: Wages are unchanged, because a king sets the price that must be paid in every manor
options.misconception: assumes a royal decree can fix a price in a market

questions.explanation: A ceiling cannot hold a price that scarcity has set, and once a third of the population is dead the workers hold the stronger hand, so the decree drove evasion, empty ploughlands, and in places flight rather than obedience. Instant obedience to a threat, a rise in output from a labour shortage, and a king's price in a market each invert what a shortage does to wages.
questions.hint: Ask who stood to lose more from the decree than the workers did.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: compute a mortality rate and read what the figure implies
questions.stem: A visitation records 1,200 souls in a village before the plague and 480 dead by the following autumn. What share of the village did the dead amount to?

options.text: Two fifths of the village, since 480 out of 1,200 is four tenths of the total
One fifth of the village, since 480 is near to 240 twice over on a guessed base
options.misconception: guesses a base figure instead of using the recorded one

options.text: Two thirds of the village, since the dead plainly exceed half the people listed
options.misconception: reads a rate of four in ten as a share above one half

options.text: Four tenths of a hundred, which is rather more than the survivors were
options.misconception: mislabels a fraction as a count and miscounts the survivors

questions.explanation: 480 dead out of 1,200 recorded is 480/1,200 = 0.4, so two in five died and about 720 were left. One fifth invents a base figure, two thirds misreads a rate of four in ten as a majority, and the last option mislabels the fraction as a count and gets the survivors wrong.
questions.hint: Divide the dead by the number recorded before, then convert the fraction.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: recall the role of the manorial reeve
questions.stem: One man is chosen to run the lord's estate, keep its account rolls, and answer for the harvest at the yearly audit. What was that officer called?

options.text: The reeve, who managed the demesne and rendered its accounts at the annual audit
The seneschal, who commanded the lord's household and ordered its supplies
options.misconception: confuses the estate manager with the household officer

options.text: The provost, who held a town's tolls and market under a royal charter
options.misconception: confuses a manorial officer with a town office

options.text: The summoner, who carried the court's writ and counted the presentment panel
options.misconception: confuses a court officer with the estate manager

questions.hint: Ask which officer rendered the account at the year's end.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state the distinction the papal claim to primacy rests on
questions.stem: A bishop of Rome argues that clerics answer to an authority kings did not create and cannot revoke. Which earlier idea is that claim built on?

options.text: That two distinct authorities exist, and the priestly one ranks above the royal in law
That the pope holds two earthly thrones, one for the west and one for the east
options.misconception: invents a second papal throne in the east

options.text: That the clergy were appointed by kings and owed their office to a royal grant
options.misconception: reverses the direction of appointment the papacy resisted

options.text: That a crown appoints a second pope in the east to balance the western one
options.misconception: invents a crown appointed counter-pope

questions.learningObjective: state the terms that ended lay investiture
questions.stem: A long quarrel over who gave a bishop his office ends in an agreement made at London. What did that agreement decide?

options.text: That the church elects bishops and the king grants only the temporal insignia
That kings appoint every bishop and the church merely pronounces them blessed
options.misconception: restores lay investiture under the name of a compromise

options.text: That bishops hold office for life and may be removed only by a papal court

options.text: That all ecclesiastical elections are suspended until the next general council

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how doctrine produced parish administrative routines
questions.stem: A priest keeps a register of baptisms and asks about kinship before marrying two people. Why does parish life generate both the register and the question?

options.text: Because rules on legitimacy and forbidden degrees made a recorded entry a legal necessity
Because the crown ordered every parish to keep a duplicate for the tax assessors
options.misconception: invents a royal tax purpose for a church register

options.text: Because guild rules fixed the dowry to be paid at every marriage in a town
options.misconception: borrows a commercial rule to explain a sacramental one

options.text: Because teachers had to count christenings each year to prove their own competence
options.misconception: invents a teaching requirement for parish records

questions.explanation: The church's own rules made these entries legal rather than devotional: a baptism record proved legitimacy and a kinship question enforced the forbidden degrees, so the routine administration followed from the doctrine it administered. A royal tax purpose, a guild dowry, and a teaching requirement each attach the routine to bodies of law the parish never served.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: read a visitation register for what it does and does not prove
questions.stem: A visitation is summarised as recording that two priests had taken fees for masses, one had not attended the synod for three years, and a third had married a woman within the forbidden degrees.

options.text: The record shows a hierarchy inspecting its clergy, so enforcement left a paper trail
The record proves none of the three priests was validly ordained in the first place
options.misconception: turns a record of misconduct into a record of invalid ordination

options.text: The record shows the parish congregation rejecting the bishop's authority outright
options.misconception: reads a list of complaints as a list of refusals

options.text: The record shows the whole clergy of the province meeting in council every year
options.misconception: turns one bishop's visitation into a provincial council

questions.explanation: A visitation naming offenders, absences, and violations is a hierarchy documenting its own supervision, and the detail matters: it proves that inspection was routine and written, not that ordination was invalid, not that a parish rejected its bishop, and not that a provincial council met each year. The register is evidence of oversight, not of the worse things a hostile reader wants from it.

options.text: Medieval assemblies had already abolished every form of taxation for good
options.misconception: invents a permanent tax abolition that never happened

questions.explanation: A century of war turns an exceptional demand into a permanent one, and the instruments available, a single levy, a manor's plough, a monastery's loan, cannot be used again on the same scale without emptying the country of the men, horses, and grain the war itself needs. A pay convention, a lost battle, and a permanent abolition of taxation each move the problem away from the recurring revenue it really was.
questions.hint: Ask whether a one-off levy can pay a war's twentieth year.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Calling a medieval government a state
questions.learningObjective: judge whether the label state fits a medieval polity
questions.stem: An essay calls a fourteenth-century kingdom a state, citing its standing administration, its taxed subjects, and its diplomatic relations. Which claim about the label is right?

options.text: The label fits if state means a durable institution, but not if it implies a modern monopoly on force
The label is wrong, because a modern state existed only after the seventeenth century
options.misconception: fixes the word to one later definition and calls everything else a fiction

options.text: The label is wrong, because medieval governments had neither officials nor taxes at all
options.misconception: denies the very features the essay's own examples name

options.text: The label is right, because a state by definition commands every soldier within its borders
options.misconception: assumes a monopoly on force the kingdom plainly lacked

questions.explanation: A medieval kingdom taxed, paid officials, kept records, and treated with its neighbours, so calling it a state fairly says that its institutions were durable; what it lacked was a modern monopoly of armed force and a uniform law, and a good definition should mark that difference. Wrong in principle, wrong in fact, and right by an anachronistic definition each fail for a different and identifiable reason.
questions.hint: Ask what part of the modern meaning the word is quietly borrowing.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A levy people would not pay
questions.learningObjective: compute a poll tax yield and judge what refusal costs
questions.stem: A crown assesses a tax of three pence on every adult in a district and counts 1,500 adults. How much has it promised itself, and what does refusal threaten?

options.text: 4,500 pence, that is 375 shillings, a yield a few refusals could defeat
1,500 pence, since the crown counts households and not every adult inside them
options.misconception: divides by three on a household basis that was not the basis

options.text: 450 pence, since the rate of three pence is applied to one adult in a hundred
options.misconception: scales a rate owed by every adult down to a small sample

options.text: 450 pounds, since three pence on fifteen hundred adults comes to that in pounds
options.misconception: reads pence as pounds by a factor of two hundred and forty

questions.explanation: Three pence on 1,500 adults is 4,500 pence, and at twelve pence to the shilling that is exactly 375 shillings, so the crown had promised itself a small return for a large act of administration and a refusal in a few villages threatened the whole yield. Counting households, applying the rate to a hundredth of the adults, and reading pence as pounds each misapply either the basis or the unit.
questions.hint: Multiply the rate by the number of people, then convert pence into shillings.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: recall what the enclosed papal election changed
questions.stem: In the later Middle Ages the cardinals meet behind locked doors, and the smoke that would signal a decision comes from one chimney. What has the practice changed?

options.text: It has closed the election to a defined body meeting in one place under a stated rule
It has ended the papal office, since a crown now chooses the successor itself
options.misconception: confuses a closed election with an appointment by a king

options.text: It has restored election by the whole church, which the cardinals have displaced
options.misconception: reads a narrow body as the voice of the whole church

options.text: It has removed the cardinals from the choice, leaving the decision to the king
options.misconception: confuses who chooses with who afterwards approves

questions.explanation: The enclosed election made the choice a matter of a defined body in a defined room under a stated rule, which is what stopped a city or a king from choosing a pope by pressure. Ending the office, restoring a universal election, and removing the cardinals each contradict the very practice the locked door describes.
questions.hint: Ask who is inside the room, and who is now outside it.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Famine and the first crisis of the century
questions.learningObjective: recall the principal fiscal effect of the great famine
questions.stem: For two summers the harvest fails across much of northern Europe and bread prices multiply. Which effect of that famine most weakened the crown's finances?

options.text: The tax base collapsed, since fewer people could pay a duty reckoned on a good harvest
The royal court was dissolved for two years, because nobody could be paid to serve
options.misconception: invents a dissolution of the court no famine record supports

options.text: The coinage was permanently withdrawn, because bad harvests leave no metal
options.misconception: confuses a failure of harvests with a loss of coin

options.text: The nobles elected their own king, because famine left the succession undecided
options.misconception: invents a succession crisis the famine did not cause

questions.explanation: A famine hits a fiscal system keyed to a good harvest: fewer carts, fewer market days, and fewer taxable transactions, so the crown's income falls in the very years it must spend. A dissolved court, a withdrawn coinage, and a noble election of a king each attach to the famine an effect it demonstrably did not have.
questions.hint: Ask what the crown's dues were reckoned upon.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: characterise a campaign directed against fellow Christians
questions.stem: A pontiff calls on rulers of the same religion as the dead to take up arms against a heretical population inside their own frontiers. What is distinctive here?

options.text: The enemy is inside the frontier, so the machinery of a holy war is turned inward
The enemy is an external power, so nothing about it differs from an earlier campaign
options.misconception: denies the inward character that defines this case

options.text: The aim is a money prize, so it is really a trading voyage in religious dress
options.misconception: reduces a religious campaign to a commercial one

options.text: The subject is the pope's own succession, so the war is really fought by clergy
options.misconception: confuses the campaign with a dispute over the papacy

questions.explanation: Turning the instruments of a holy war on a population inside the frontier is what makes this case distinctive: the callers were Christians, the targets were Christians, and the outcome was territorial annexation and a permanent church presence in the county. An external enemy, a commercial prize, and a war over the papacy each deny the defining feature.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the frontier the target stood on.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the label black death leaves out
questions.learningObjective: reason about what a name conceals in a demographic shock
questions.stem: Everyone calls the plague of 1347 the Black Death, and then reads the period as a collapse. Why is the name itself part of the problem?

options.text: It fixes attention on the disease, so the wage rises and bargaining power it gave workers go unnoticed
It is too vague, because the word death conceals which disease actually killed the victims
options.misconception: objects to the vagueness of a name instead of its framing

options.text: It is too dramatic, because the outbreak killed far fewer people than later writers claimed
options.misconception: claims the mortality figure was exaggerated without any support

options.text: It is too narrow, because the crisis also involved a war fought at the very same time
options.misconception: tacks a war onto a demographic argument it does not belong in

questions.explanation: The name points at the pathogen, which invites a reader to stop at the dying and miss what the dying did: with a third of the people gone, the survivors could set terms, and that is the social history inside the demographic one. Vagueness about the disease, exaggeration of the toll, and a war tacked on to explain the same decades each leave the labour question untouched.
questions.hint: Ask what the survivors could do once the dead had been counted.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: read a chronicle summary as evidence with clear limits
questions.stem: A chronicler's entry is summarised as recording that the sickness came in the autumn, that the sick were buried without priest or bell, and that the carts could not carry the dead away fast enough. What can this support?

options.text: That contemporaries saw the scale of the dying and the collapse of ordinary arrangements around it
That the chronicler counted the dead accurately, since his figures are exact to the unit
options.misconception: reads an impressionistic entry as a verified count

options.text: That the parish clergy refused to bury the dead for reasons of their own
options.misconception: reads a shortage of survivors as a deliberate clerical refusal

options.text: That the carts were inadequate because the roads had been abandoned altogether
options.misconception: explains a stated collapse by a cause the entry never mentions

questions.explanation: The entry is evidence that contemporaries registered a catastrophe, because the burial and transport arrangements it names were the ones that had failed, which is a strong claim about perception and a weak one about a precise total. It is not a verified count, not proof of a clerical refusal, and not a statement about roads, and a reader who wants those has to look elsewhere.
questions.hint: Ask whether the entry is evidence of the scale measured or of the scale felt.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how the collapse of a credit convention destabilised states
questions.stem: A great banking house fails, its paper obligations are called in doubt, and lenders across three kingdoms cut their limits. Why does one firm's failure reach so far?

options.text: The paper was a promise to the state as much as to a creditor, so the state lost its means of payment at once
The firm's branches were the only ships then carrying goods between the ports
options.misconception: invents a shipping monopoly no house of the period held

options.text: The state had guaranteed every note, so it owed the whole of the loss at once
options.misconception: turns a credit convention into a state guarantee of each note

options.text: The failure ended the silver supply, so no metal was left anywhere to coin
options.misconception: confuses a bank's own balance sheet with the money supply

questions.explanation: The reach of the failure shows that the paper was a public instrument as much as a private one, since states had settled their accounts in it and financed war with it, so when it was doubted the government lost its means of payment as well as its credit. A shipping monopoly, a guarantee of every note, and a vanished silver supply each misplace the mechanism the collapse revealed.
questions.hint: Ask what the states had been using to pay their soldiers.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Which pressure did most to erode the medieval order
questions.learningObjective: weigh rival accounts of the weakening of a late medieval order
questions.stem: Four explanations compete for the weakening of the late medieval order: money and credit, the Church's own decay, the rise of the towns, and the pressure of war. Which fits the evidence best?

options.text: A combination, since each of the four weakened the others and none of them explains the result alone
Money and credit alone, since the other three were consequences of a failing currency
options.misconception: makes one factor total and treats the rest as derivative

options.text: The towns alone, since the Church and the currency were irrelevant to urban growth
options.misconception: makes one factor total and dismisses two institutions outright

options.text: War alone, since the first three predate the wars and so cannot explain them
options.misconception: confuses what came before the wars with what cannot cause them

questions.explanation: The record shows the four working together: towns used the credit, the Church's decay loosened the institutions that had policed trade, and the wars consumed what the others produced, so each is cause and consequence. Any single factor made total, and the claim that a thing predates the wars cannot be the cause, both overstate one and misjudge the relation.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four used the others' output.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: connect a coinage change to the movement of a price series
questions.stem: A government halves the silver in its coinage while leaving the face value the same, and a market record shows wheat rising from 8 to 20 shillings a bushel. What does the pair show?

options.text: A rise of 150 per cent, which is roughly what halving the metal in fixed-value coin predicts
A rise of 250 per cent, since the bushel simply went from 8 to 20 and both are added
options.misconception: treats a ratio as a sum and loses the starting price

options.text: A rise of 12 per cent, since 20 minus 8 is simply taken as the percentage itself
options.misconception: confuses a difference of twelve with a rate of twelve per cent

options.text: A rise of 20 per cent, since the new price is read as the whole of the increase
options.misconception: reads the ending level as the size of the change

questions.explanation: The rise is (20 - 8) / 8 = 1.5, that is 150 per cent, and that is the order of magnitude expected when the silver in the coin is halved while the face value is held fixed, which is why a debasement shows up in a price series at all. Adding the two prices, reading twelve as a percentage, and reading twenty as the change each misread the arithmetic.
questions.hint: Compute the rise as a share of the starting price, not of the new one.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Dating the end of the Middle Ages
questions.learningObjective: explain why period boundaries are conventional choices
questions.stem: Two textbooks close the Middle Ages in different years and neither cites a different fact. Why is that not a mistake that one of them can fix?

options.text: A boundary is a choice about which change counts as a break, and the facts support several choices
One textbook is older, and the older date is automatically the correct one
options.misconception: settles a scholarly choice by seniority alone

options.text: The facts are still disputed, so nobody has yet managed to count them properly
options.misconception: turns a choice of definition into an error in counting

options.text: Dates matter only to chronology, and chronology is not part of history at all
options.misconception: dismisses the whole question as a technicality

questions.explanation: Periodising is an argument about which change deserves to begin a new account, and the candidates, a city's fall, a voyage, a plough, an event in a single place, each pick something real while leaving other continuities running straight through. Seniority, a miscount, and the irrelevance of chronology each dodge the choice the textbook actually made.
questions.hint: Ask which change each date is claiming deserves to begin an account.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of a linked decline
questions.learningObjective: sequence pressures that feed one another over a century
questions.stem: Four developments feed one another over a single century. Put them in the order a defensible sequence would run.

options.text: A silver shortage leaves the towns unable to pay, and credit to them contracts
options.misconception: starts with the money shortage, which was a later consequence of the credit

options.text: A currency debased to pay a war is refused abroad, and that refusal closes the market
options.misconception: closes the market before the debasement that foreigners were refusing to take

options.text: Rulers borrow from merchants against the customs of a growing overseas trade
options.misconception: puts the credit contraction before the borrowing that created the exposure

options.text: War after war is financed by borrowing against receipts that have not yet come in
options.misconception: makes the wars the first step, though the customs had to exist to be lent against

questions.explanation: The chain runs from collateral to debt: growing customs gave rulers something to borrow against, war turned that collateral into a debt, the silver shortage then tightened the credit those debts rested on, and the debasement that paid the debt was refused abroad, which shut the market the collateral had come from. The tempting orders put the contraction first, make the wars the origin, move the shortage to the front, or close the market before the debasement that closed it.
questions.hint: Ask what the creditors held in their hands before they lent.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: infer a structural change from a change in how force was obtained
questions.stem: By the later fifteenth century a lord's power rests on a small body of paid men-at-arms and on cannon set in a tower. Which change does this show most clearly?

options.text: Force that is simply purchased, replacing the service that landholding had obliged
A revived oath of homage, now sworn to a king rather than to a lord
options.misconception: reads a purchased force as a revived personal oath

options.text: The end of all landholding, since nobody any longer holds land for service
options.misconception: infers an end to tenure from a change in military employment

options.text: The disappearance of the manor, since the fields must have been abandoned too
options.misconception: infers an end to the manor from a change in defence

questions.explanation: Paying soldiers and mounting cannon are purchases, so the power behind the lord is no longer the land that obliged him to serve, and tenure, homage, and the manor all survive in weakened form beside the new force. A revived oath, an end to all landholding, and an abandoned manor each infer much more than the change in defence supports.
questions.hint: Ask whether the men in the tower were paid or were owing service.
